ch04.card: Part 3 of 8. The thinker: rounds of looking and passing notes.
ch04.s01.c1: This is the thinker, the second part of the model. It does the thinking.
ch04.s01.c2: It is ours. It starts from scratch and learns only from our practice.
ch04.s01.c3: The planned size is about 100 million numbers. That size has never been tested.
ch04.s02.c1: Picture only. Think of a small team of note-takers around one question.
ch04.s02.c2: Each round, every note-taker looks at the whole question again.
ch04.s02.c3: Then they pass notes to each other and write down what they now believe.
ch04.s02.c4: The same team, with the same habits, every round.
ch04.s03.c1: A vector is a list of numbers, like a note card with a row of numbers.
ch04.s03.c2: The thinker keeps 8 control vectors. Two of them steer the work.
ch04.s03.c3: It also keeps 36 memory vectors, where its notes are kept.
ch04.s03.c4: Older builds had 17 vectors: 8 control and 9 memory.
ch04.s04.c1: After each round from round 2 on, the call writer reads control vector 0. That part was tested in an older design.
ch04.s04.c2: It either writes a request for the calculator, like sub 12 5, or writes nothing.
ch04.s04.c3: The numbers in the request are usually copied from the question or an earlier reply.
ch04.s05.c1: Controls 2 to 7 feed no output. They only pass information along when the notes look at each other.
ch04.s05.c2: In an older build, switching them off at test time cost 1.6 points on the main test.
ch04.s05.c3: On the multi-step test they cost 7.8 points: 99.4 fell to 91.6.
ch04.s05.c4: Those numbers are one copy, seed 200. All six copies of that older design lost points, very unevenly.
ch04.s06.c1: Each letter of the question is one box. A borrowed reader, Gemma, has already given each letter its meaning.
ch04.s06.c2: Each note vector looks at every letter. In later rounds it also looks at every calculator reply.
ch04.s06.c3: The shading inside each note is a picture only, not real numbers.
ch04.s07.c1: Step 2: the note vectors look at each other. In code this is called self-attention.
ch04.s07.c2: Each note reads the other notes and keeps what matters from them.
ch04.s07.c3: The letters are not compared with each other inside the thinker.
ch04.s07.c4: Step 3: each note goes through a small network.
ch04.s07.c5: At the 100M step, it widens to 4.8 times as many numbers, then squeezes back down.
ch04.s07.c6: Then the notes go on to the next round.
ch04.s08.c1: One look, compare and think unit is a block. The same blocks run in every round.
ch04.s08.c2: The learned numbers are the same in every round. Same team, same habits.
ch04.s08.c3: A round stamp, a learned tag for the round number, is added to the notes each round. The older design ran this way.
ch04.s09.c1: Tom has 12 apples, gives away 5, then buys 3. After round 2, the call writer writes sub 12 5.
ch04.s09.c2: It copies 12 and 5 from the question. The calculator replies 7, which is added to the notes.
ch04.s09.c3: Round 3 sees that reply. After it, the call writer writes add 7 3, and the calculator replies 10.
ch04.s09.c4: The talker, which writes the final answer, copies 10 from the last reply. A worked example, traced from the code, never run as a whole.
ch04.s10.c1: After each round, a tiny learned stop switch, the bell, asks: is this settled, or should it think more?
ch04.s10.c2: It must think at least 1 round. It can never go past 32 rounds.
ch04.s10.c3: It learns from a settled label: stop once no later round would have been right. It is built, but never run.
ch04.s11.c1: A block is one look, compare and think unit, built from attention and a small network.
ch04.s11.c2: Count every learned number in one block, where each vector is 512 numbers wide. It comes to about 4.62 million.
ch04.s11.c3: By our arithmetic, 21 blocks alone give 97.1 million. An older plan said 30 blocks, which would give about 139 million.
ch04.s12.c1: The learned part of the model comes in four sizes, named 3M, 10M, 30M and 100M for their rough size.
ch04.s12.c2: These are counts from the build. The finished design, B3, has not been run at any of these sizes yet.
ch04.s12.c3: As built so far, without the planned talker, the whole model at the 100 million step is 373.1 million numbers, borrowed reader included.
ch04.s13.c1: An average question has 81 letters. Every letter against every letter is 81 times 81, or 6,561 checks.
ch04.s13.c2: Notes look at letters instead. A rough count: 44 notes, each looking at 81 letters and 27 number slots, is 4,752 checks per round.
ch04.s13.c3: Over 8 rounds, the older count, that is 4,752 times 8, or 38,016. At 81 letters, no work is saved.
ch04.s13.c4: Its gain is structure, not speed. By this count, much longer text would favour the notes, but that is untested.
ch04.s14.c1: In the first completed test, on an older design, one copy at the smallest size scored 73.01 points out of 100, thinking on, on 6,040 kept-aside questions.
ch04.s14.c2: With thinking switched off, zero rounds, the same copy scored 0.66 points.
ch04.s14.c3: That is one copy at one size. Part 8 explains the test and its checks.
ch04.s15.c1: Not known: the thinker has never been tested at 100 million numbers.
ch04.s15.c2: Not known: whether many rounds hurt. One older probe, on one seed, found 16 rounds cost 1.2 to 1.9 points.
ch04.s15.c3: Experts, many small specialist networks with a few used at a time, are a separate idea, not yet tested and not covered here.
ch04.s15.c4: Remember: the thinker looks, passes notes and thinks, in rounds. The same blocks run every round. A learned bell is built to say when to stop.
